draft.title: Aerobic cellular respiration
card: Aerobic cellular respiration releases energy from glucose and stores it in ATP, using oxygen. Overall: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP.
Glycolysis
happens in the cytosol. Glucose is split into two pyruvate molecules, making a small net gain of 2 ATP. It does not need oxygen.
Krebs cycle
happens in the mitochondrial matrix. Pyruvate is broken down, releasing carbon dioxide and loading carriers (NADH and FADH2) with energy, with 2 ATP made.
Electron transport chain
on the inner mitochondrial membrane. The carriers deliver electrons, and oxygen accepts them at the end to form water. This stage makes most of the ATP, so the total is about 30 to 32 per glucose.
draft.remember: Three stages, one goal: glucose energy into ATP, with most ATP made at the electron transport chain.

a.q: Which stage of aerobic respiration makes most of the ATP?
opts: The electron transport chain
Glycolysis
The Krebs cycle
The splitting of glucose into pyruvate
a.why: The electron transport chain uses energy from the loaded carriers to make most of the ATP, about 26 to 28 of the total. Glycolysis is tempting because it comes first, but it gains only a net 2 ATP.
a.clue: Think about where the loaded carriers deliver their electrons.

b.q: A drug stops oxygen from accepting electrons at the end of the electron transport chain in a muscle cell's mitochondria. Why would ATP production by aerobic respiration fall sharply?
opts: The chain stops, so the carriers cannot be unloaded
Glucose can no longer be split into pyruvate in the cytosol
Carbon dioxide can no longer be released by the cell
Water is needed to start the Krebs cycle in the matrix
b.why: If oxygen cannot accept electrons, the chain backs up and the carriers stay loaded. Most ATP is made at this stage, so output falls sharply. Glycolysis is not the problem, because it does not need oxygen.
b.clue: Which stage uses oxygen, and what must the carriers do there?

b.best: The chain stops, so the carriers cannot be unloaded

problems.detail: Two options, 'The splitting of glucose into pyruvate' and 'Glycolysis', describe the same stage, so a student can rule both out and the question has only three real choices.
